frase_gancho.texto: A king with curls and a serpent headdress tramples his bound enemy.

puente_narrativo.texto: Captives also appeared on the ball court. Look for a stone disk with a player resting on one knee, striking a ball with his hip.

guion_corto.texto: This limestone stela is more than three meters tall and was erected in the year 731 in Calakmul, in Campeche. It shows King Yuknoom Took Kawiil in profile, standing over a captive with his hands tied. He wears armor made of plates and a long cape, and he holds a spear. His headdress is a serpent with open jaws, from which the king’s head seems to emerge. Notice one unusual detail: he wears his hair in curls on both sides of his face. It is the portrait of a powerful ruler, and a warning: this is how the enemies of Calakmul are treated. This piece was looted in the twentieth century and later recovered.

guion_largo.texto:
A stone king looks straight ahead. At his feet lies a defeated enemy. Behind him, the serpent that serves as his crown. The scene seems simple, but it holds one of the greatest rivalries of the Maya world: that of Calakmul and Tikal.

Calakmul, deep in the jungle of Campeche, was one of the most powerful cities of the Maya world. Its name means something like “two neighboring mounds,” and it was given by the botanist Cyrus Lundell, who found it in 1931. It was the capital of the Snake kingdom, which gathered allies across the whole region. Its great rival was Tikal, in Guatemala. I already told you about Tikal in the Teotihuacán Hall: there, in January of the year 378, Maya inscriptions record the arrival of the general Siyaj Kak, “Fire Is Born,” linked to Teotihuacán. The two kingdoms clashed for generations, like two great blocs.

The name of the kingdom, Kaan, means “serpent” in the Maya language, and that is where the headdress comes from: the king emerges from the jaws of the serpent that gives its name to his dynasty, as if that animal were his emblem and his origin. Calakmul came to have more than a hundred stelae, the largest collection of monuments of this kind in a single Maya city.

Here, King Yuknoom Took Kawiil appears in the year 731. A few decades earlier, Tikal had defeated Calakmul in an important battle. And even so, the king had himself portrayed in full strength. It is propaganda, just like the kind you saw with [the Dancers](mna_s07_danzante_montealban) of Monte Albán and the [Stone of Tízoc](mna_s06_tizoc): power is displayed with captives.

Each stela was dedicated on an important date of the calendar, with a ceremony. It is thought that the monument was considered almost a living being, one that received offerings and, at times, even a name of its own.

Look at the captive, at the king’s feet. The Maya waged wars to capture nobles from other cities, who were then humiliated and, at times, sacrificed. An important captive was worth more than a territory. That is why he appears here: he is a trophy.

And then the curls. It is a very rare feature in Maya art, and nobody knows for sure why it appears. It may be an ornament, a wig, or a fashion at court. But it makes this portrait unmistakable.

The modern history of the stela also deserves to be told. In the twentieth century, looters cut it with saws to reduce its thickness and smuggle it out. It lost part of the stone, and with it, some glyphs on the sides. It was recovered and brought to the capital. Today it appears whole, but with scars. That is why it matters so much that pieces be studied in their place of origin: what is lost in a looting cannot be recovered.

Finally, imagine the plaza where it once stood: an enormous pyramid, about forty-five meters tall, behind it, and the stela in front, perhaps painted in bright colors, alongside dozens of others. Today it is a place of silence, in a protected nature reserve. But thirteen hundred years ago, this stone was a shout.

texto: Look for the curls on both sides of the king’s face
Find the bound captive beneath the king’s feet
Observe the serpent jaws that form his headdress

texto.pregunta: Myth: Maya stelae were just decorations, with no texts.
texto.respuesta: Reality: They bore the names, dates, and deeds of kings: they were pages of history in stone.
